description: Evidence Coach golden set: resistance training, protein and body-composition nutrition. Reference answers paraphrase ISSN / ACSM / NSCA position stands and well-known meta-analyses. key_studies[].id_confidence: verified = identifier confirmed by web search while authoring (2026-10-19); high = recalled with high confidence; medium = recalled, probably right; unverified = do not rely on the identifier (excluded from coverage). Numbers are only given where the source states them; see notes for uncertainty.

items.question: How many sets per week should I do per muscle for hypertrophy?

reference.recommendation: Do at least about 10 hard sets per muscle per week; more weekly sets generally produce more growth, with diminishing returns at higher volumes. Roughly 10-20 weekly sets per muscle is a reasonable range for most trained lifters.
key_points: A graded dose-response: more weekly sets per muscle produce more hypertrophy.
10 or more weekly sets per muscle produced larger gains than fewer than 5 (Schoenfeld 2017).
Each additional weekly set was associated with roughly 0.37% more growth in the 2017 meta-analysis.
Returns diminish at high volumes; the upper limit is debated.

key_studies.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW. Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sports Sci. 2017;35(11):1073-1082.
Schoenfeld BJ, Contreras B, Krieger J, et al. Resistance training volume enhances muscle hypertrophy but not strength in trained men. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019;51(1):94-103.

Pelland JC, Remmert JF, Robinson ZP, et al. The resistance training dose response: meta-regressions exploring the effects of weekly volume and frequency on muscle hypertrophy and strength gain. SportRxiv preprint 2024 (later in Sports Med).

items.source: Schoenfeld, Ogborn & Krieger 2017 (J Sports Sci) meta-analysis
items.notes: Whether gains keep rising above ~20 sets is contested (see vol-upper-limit), so leaning is the best status; consensus is accepted because the dose-response itself is well supported.

items.question: Is doing more than 20 hard sets per muscle per week better for muscle growth than staying around 10 to 20?

reference.recommendation: The evidence is split: some trials in trained lifters found more growth with very high volumes, while meta-regressions suggest diminishing returns as volume rises. Going beyond about 20 weekly sets may add a little growth for some advanced lifters at a large time and recovery cost; it is a reasonable individual choice rather than a requirement.
key_points: Very-high-volume trials in trained men (e.g. Schoenfeld 2019) reported more growth with the highest volume.
Pooled dose-response analyses show diminishing returns per extra set at higher volumes.
Measurement issues (muscle swelling, short trials) make very-high-volume results uncertain.

key_numbers.context: commonly cited upper end of the evidence-supported range

key_studies.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Contreras B, Krieger J, et al. Resistance training volume enhances muscle hypertrophy but not strength in trained men. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019;51(1):94-103.
Baz-Valle E, Balsalobre-Fernandez C, Alix-Fages C, Santos-Concejero J. A systematic review of the effects of different resistance training volumes on muscle hypertrophy. J Hum Kinet. 2022;81:199-210.
Pelland JC et al. The resistance training dose response (meta-regressions). SportRxiv 2024.

items.source: Schoenfeld 2019 (MSSE); Pelland et al. 2024 dose-response meta-regressions
items.notes: Several high-volume trials from one group were later retracted; do not use retracted work as a reference.

items.question: If my total weekly sets are the same, should I train each muscle once or twice a week?

reference.recommendation: When weekly volume is equated, training frequency makes little or no difference to hypertrophy, so choose whatever frequency lets you do your sets with good quality; splitting high volumes over 2 or more sessions per muscle is a practical way to keep set quality up.
key_points: Volume-equated meta-analysis: no significant difference between higher and lower frequencies (Schoenfeld 2019).
Without volume equated, training a muscle at least twice per week produced more growth than once (Schoenfeld 2016).
Frequency is mainly a tool to distribute volume.

key_numbers.context: at least twice weekly when volume is not equated (2016 meta-analysis)

key_studies.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J, Krieger J. How many times per week should a muscle be trained to maximize muscle hypertrophy? A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies examining the effects of resistance training frequency. J Sports Sci. 2019;37(11):1286-1295.
Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW. Effects of resistance training frequency on measures of muscle hypertrophy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2016;46(11):1689-1697.

items.source: Schoenfeld, Grgic & Krieger 2019 (J Sports Sci) meta-analysis

items.question: Do I need to train to failure to build muscle?

reference.recommendation: No. Training to momentary failure is not required; sets stopped a few reps short of failure produce similar hypertrophy in meta-analyses. Sets should still be hard (roughly 0-3 reps in reserve), since growth appears to increase as sets get closer to failure.
key_points: Grgic 2022: no significant hypertrophy difference between failure and non-failure training (ES 0.22, CI crossing zero).
Refalo 2023: a trivial pooled effect favouring failure (ES 0.19), no advantage of momentary failure over non-failure in subgroup analyses; possibly non-linear relationship.
Dose-response meta-regressions suggest hypertrophy rises as proximity to failure increases, while strength does not depend on it much.

key_numbers.context: Refalo 2023 pooled set-failure vs non-failure, described as trivial

key_studies.citation: Refalo MC, Helms ER, Trexler ET, Hamilton DL, Fyfe JJ. Influence of resistance training proximity-to-failure on skeletal muscle hypertrophy: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023;53(3):649-665.

Grgic J, Schoenfeld BJ, Orazem J, Sabol F. Effects of resistance training performed to repetition failure or non-failure on muscular strength and hypertrophy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sport Health Sci. 2022;11(2):202-211.

Robinson ZP, Pelland JC, Remmert JF, et al. Exploring the dose-response relationship between estimated resistance training proximity to failure, strength gain, and muscle hypertrophy: a series of meta-regressions. Sports Med. 2024.

items.source: Refalo et al. 2023 (Sports Med); Grgic et al. 2022 (J Sport Health Sci)
items.notes: Refalo DOI and Grgic bibliographic details confirmed by web search (PMIDs not confirmed). Status is borderline between consensus (failure not required) and leaning (closer to failure may be better).

items.question: Is training to failure necessary for strength gains?

reference.recommendation: No. Strength gains are similar whether or not sets are taken to failure, so heavy sets stopped short of failure are sufficient and limit fatigue.
key_points: Grgic 2022: no significant strength difference between failure and non-failure training (ES -0.09).
Strength gain appears largely insensitive to proximity to failure in dose-response analyses.

key_studies.citation: Grgic J, Schoenfeld BJ, Orazem J, Sabol F. Effects of resistance training performed to repetition failure or non-failure on muscular strength and hypertrophy. J Sport Health Sci. 2022;11(2):202-211.
Robinson ZP et al. Proximity to failure meta-regressions. Sports Med. 2024.

items.source: Grgic et al. 2022 (J Sport Health Sci)

items.question: Do I need heavy weights to build muscle, or can light weights work just as well?

reference.recommendation: Light and heavy loads build similar muscle when sets are taken close to failure (from roughly 30% of 1RM upward); heavy loads are better for maximal strength.
key_points: Low- vs high-load meta-analysis: similar hypertrophy, greater 1RM strength with high loads (Schoenfeld 2017).
Network meta-analysis (Lopez 2021): similar hypertrophy across load ranges; strength favours higher loads.

key_numbers.context: approximate lower bound of loads shown to build muscle when taken near failure

key_studies.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J, Ogborn D, Krieger JW. Strength and hypertrophy adaptations between low- vs. high-load resistance training: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res. 2017;31(12):3508-3523.

Lopez P, Radaelli R, Taaffe DR, et al. Resistance training load effects on muscle hypertrophy and strength gain: systematic review and network meta-analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2021;53(6):1206-1216.

items.source: Schoenfeld et al. 2017 (J Strength Cond Res) meta-analysis

items.question: What loads and rep ranges are best for increasing my one-rep max?

reference.recommendation: Train mostly with heavy loads: ACSM recommends about 60-70% of 1RM for 8-12 reps for novices and progressing to 80-100% of 1RM for advanced lifters seeking maximal strength. Heavy loads produce greater 1RM gains than light loads.
key_points: Strength is specific to the load trained: heavier loads give larger 1RM improvements (Schoenfeld 2017).
ACSM 2009 progression models: novices 60-70% 1RM for 8-12 reps; advanced 80-100% 1RM.

key_numbers.context: ACSM advanced loading for maximal strength

key_studies.citation: American College of Sports Medicine. Position stand: progression models in resistance training for healthy adults. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2009;41(3):687-708.
Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J, Ogborn D, Krieger JW. Strength and hypertrophy adaptations between low- vs. high-load resistance training. J Strength Cond Res. 2017;31(12):3508-3523.

items.source: ACSM 2009 position stand: progression models in resistance training

items.question: What is the minimum amount of training I need to keep getting stronger as a trained lifter?

reference.recommendation: Strength can increase with very little training: a single set of 6-12 reps at 70-85% of 1RM, 2-3 times per week for 8-12 weeks increased 1RM in trained men, though more volume generally yields more.
key_points: Minimum-dose meta-analysis in resistance-trained men (Androulakis-Korakakis 2020).
Higher volumes produce larger gains, so the minimum is for maintenance or busy periods.

key_studies.citation: Androulakis-Korakakis P, Fisher JP, Steele J. The minimum effective training dose required to increase 1RM strength in resistance-trained men: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2020;50(4):751-765.

items.source: Androulakis-Korakakis, Fisher & Steele 2020 (Sports Med)
items.notes: Population is resistance-trained men; generalising to women is an extrapolation.

items.question: How long should I rest between sets to maximize muscle growth?

reference.recommendation: Rest at least about 1.5-2 minutes between sets, especially on multi-joint exercises; very short rests (around 1 minute or less) tend to reduce volume and may slightly reduce growth, while going beyond about 2-3 minutes adds little.
key_points: Schoenfeld 2016: 3-minute rests produced more strength and some measures of hypertrophy than 1-minute rests in trained men.
Bayesian meta-analysis (Singer 2024): a small benefit of resting more than 60 s, little difference beyond about 90 s.

key_studies.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Pope ZK, Benik FM, et al. Longer interset rest periods enhance muscle strength and hypertrophy in resistance-trained men. J Strength Cond Res. 2016;30(7):1805-1812.

Singer A, Wolf M, Generoso L, et al. Give it a rest: a systematic review with Bayesian meta-analysis on the effect of inter-set rest interval duration on muscle hypertrophy. Front Sports Act Living. 2024;6:1429789.

items.source: Schoenfeld et al. 2016 (J Strength Cond Res); Singer et al. 2024 (Front Sports Act Living)
items.notes: Exact thresholds (90 s vs 2 min) are uncertain; the agreement judge should accept any recommendation of moderate-to-long rests.

items.question: Are partial reps at long muscle lengths as good as full range of motion for muscle growth?

reference.recommendation: Full range of motion is a safe default and generally builds at least as much muscle as partials, but partials performed at long muscle lengths appear similar or possibly better in some studies; the evidence is limited and mixed.
key_points: Meta-analyses find full ROM similar to or better than partial ROM overall, especially for lower-body hypertrophy.
Training at long muscle lengths (lengthened partials) may produce similar or greater growth than short-length partials and sometimes full ROM.
Few studies, mostly short and in untrained people.

key_studies.citation: Pallares JG, Hernandez-Belmonte A, Martinez-Cava A, et al. Effects of range of motion on resistance training adaptations: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2021;31(10):1866-1881.
Wolf M, Androulakis-Korakakis P, Fisher J, Schoenfeld B, Steele J. Partial vs full range of motion resistance training: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Int J Strength Cond. 2023;3(1).

items.source: Pallares et al. 2021; Wolf et al. 2023 meta-analyses
items.notes: No key numbers on purpose: effect estimates differ by analysis. Identifiers not verified.

items.question: Does periodized training (linear or undulating) build more muscle than non-periodized training?

reference.recommendation: For hypertrophy, periodized and non-periodized programs give similar results when volume is equated, and linear vs undulating models do not differ meaningfully; periodization may give a small advantage for maximal strength.
key_points: Linear vs daily undulating periodization: no meaningful difference in hypertrophy (Grgic 2017).
Volume-equated meta-analysis (Moesgaard 2022): periodization favoured strength slightly, not hypertrophy.

key_studies.citation: Grgic J, Mikulic P, Podnar H, Pedisic Z. Effects of linear and daily undulating periodized resistance training programs on measures of muscle hypertrophy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. PeerJ. 2017;5:e3695.

Moesgaard L, Beck MM, Christiansen L, Aagaard P, Lundbye-Jensen J. Effects of periodization on strength and muscle hypertrophy in volume-equated resistance training programs: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2022;52(7):1647-1666.

items.source: Grgic et al. 2017 (PeerJ); Moesgaard et al. 2022 (Sports Med)

items.question: Will doing cardio alongside lifting hurt my muscle and strength gains?

reference.recommendation: Moderate cardio does not meaningfully reduce hypertrophy or maximal strength for most people, but it can blunt explosive strength/power; interference is more likely with running, high cardio frequency or duration, and when cardio is done right before lifting.
key_points: Updated meta-analysis (Schumann 2022): concurrent training did not compromise hypertrophy or maximal strength, but attenuated explosive strength.
Wilson 2012: interference depends on modality (running worse than cycling), frequency and duration.

key_studies.citation: Wilson JM, Marin PJ, Rhea MR, et al. Concurrent training: a meta-analysis examining interference of aerobic and resistance exercises. J Strength Cond Res. 2012;26(8):2293-2307.

Schumann M, Feuerbacher JF, Sunkeler M, et al. Compatibility of concurrent aerobic and strength training for skeletal muscle size and function: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2022;52(3):601-612.

items.source: Schumann et al. 2022 (Sports Med); Wilson et al. 2012 (J Strength Cond Res)

items.question: Do women need to train differently from men to build muscle and strength?

reference.recommendation: No fundamentally different approach is needed: women gain muscle at similar relative rates to men and can gain relative upper-body strength at similar or greater rates, so the same principles of volume, effort and progression apply.
key_points: Meta-analysis (Roberts 2020): similar relative hypertrophy between sexes; greater relative upper-body strength gains in women.
Most training studies are in men, so some programming details are extrapolated.

key_studies.citation: Roberts BM, Nuckols G, Krieger JW. Sex differences in resistance training: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res. 2020;34(5):1448-1460.

items.source: Roberts, Nuckols & Krieger 2020 (J Strength Cond Res)

items.question: I'm 68. Can I still build muscle with weights, and how should I train?

reference.recommendation: Yes. Resistance training reliably increases muscle mass and strength in older adults; train each major muscle group about 2-3 times per week with progressive loading, starting light and building up.
key_points: Meta-analysis in aging adults: resistance training increased lean body mass by about 1.1 kg on average (Peterson 2011).
NSCA position statement (Fragala 2019): 2-3 sessions per week of progressive multi-joint training, with power training, is effective and safe for healthy older adults.

key_studies.citation: Peterson MD, Sen A, Gordon PM. Influence of resistance exercise on lean body mass in aging adults: a meta-analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2011;43(2):249-258.
Fragala MS, Cadore EL, Dorgo S, et al. Resistance training for older adults: position statement from the National Strength and Conditioning Association. J Strength Cond Res. 2019;33(8):2019-2052.

items.source: NSCA position statement 2019 (Fragala et al.); Peterson et al. 2011 meta-analysis
items.notes: The 1.1 kg figure is recalled from the Peterson 2011 abstract (medium confidence).

items.question: Does blood-flow restriction training with light weights build as much muscle as heavy lifting?

reference.recommendation: Low-load blood-flow restriction training (roughly 20-40% of 1RM) produces hypertrophy similar to heavy training, but heavy training produces larger strength gains.
key_points: Meta-analysis (Lixandrao 2018): similar hypertrophy between low-load BFR and high-load training; greater strength with high loads.
Position stand (Patterson 2019): loads of about 20-40% 1RM with appropriate cuff pressures.

key_studies.citation: Lixandrao ME, Ugrinowitsch C, Berton R, et al. Magnitude of muscle strength and mass adaptations between high-load resistance training versus low-load resistance training associated with blood-flow restriction: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2018;48(2):361-378.
Patterson SD, Hughes L, Warmington S, et al. Blood flow restriction exercise: considerations of methodology, application, and safety. Front Physiol. 2019;10:533.

items.source: Lixandrao et al. 2018 (Sports Med); Patterson et al. 2019 position stand

items.question: Are free weights better than machines for building muscle?

reference.recommendation: Both build muscle similarly; choose based on preference, access and comfort. Strength gains are specific to the modality you test on.
key_points: Meta-analysis (Haugen 2023): no meaningful difference in hypertrophy between free-weight and machine training; strength gains favour the trained modality.

key_studies.citation: Haugen ME, Vasenden-Hauge V, Haugen KL, et al. Free-weight resistance training versus machine resistance training: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2023;15:103.

items.source: Haugen et al. 2023 meta-analysis (BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil)

items.question: Should I progress by adding weight or by adding reps to keep building muscle?

reference.recommendation: Either works for hypertrophy: progressing load or progressing repetitions produced similar muscle growth, with load progression perhaps slightly better for 1RM strength.
key_points: Plotkin 2022 RCT: similar hypertrophy with load or repetition progression in trained individuals.

key_studies.citation: Plotkin D, Coleman M, Van Every D, et al. Progressive overload without progressing load? The effects of load or repetition progression on muscular adaptations. PeerJ. 2022;10:e14142.

items.source: Plotkin et al. 2022 (PeerJ)

items.question: Does static stretching before lifting reduce my strength?

reference.recommendation: Short static stretches (under about 60 seconds per muscle) within a full warm-up have trivial effects on strength; long static stretching right before lifting can reduce performance, so keep it brief or move it elsewhere.
key_points: Behm 2016 review: static stretching under 60 s per muscle has small to trivial performance impairments, longer durations larger impairments.

key_numbers.context: threshold below which effects are trivial

key_studies.citation: Behm DG, Blazevich AJ, Kay AD, McHugh M. Acute effects of muscle stretching on physical performance, range of motion, and injury incidence in healthy active individuals: a systematic review. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2016;41(1):1-11.

items.source: Behm et al. 2016 (Appl Physiol Nutr Metab)

items.question: How much protein do I need per day to build muscle?

reference.recommendation: About 1.6 g of protein per kg of body weight per day maximizes resistance-training gains for most people; going up to about 2.2 g/kg/day covers individual variation. The ISSN recommends 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day for most exercising individuals.
key_points: Morton 2018 meta-regression: gains in fat-free mass plateaued at about 1.62 g/kg/day (95% CI upper bound about 2.2).
ISSN 2017 position stand: 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day for most exercising individuals.
Protein supplementation adds little once total intake is adequate.

key_studies.citation: Morton RW, Murphy KT, McKellar SR, et al. A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(6):376-384.
Jager R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20.

Nunes EA, Colenso-Semple L, McKellar SR, et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults. J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle. 2022;13(2):795-810.

items.source: Morton et al. 2018 (Br J Sports Med); ISSN position stand: protein and exercise (Jager et al. 2017)

items.question: How much protein should I eat on a cut to keep my muscle?

reference.recommendation: Eat more protein than at maintenance: roughly 1.6-2.2 g/kg of body weight per day at minimum, and for lean, trained lifters in a deficit about 2.3-3.1 g/kg of fat-free mass per day, combined with continued resistance training.
key_points: Helms 2014 systematic review: 2.3-3.1 g/kg of fat-free mass for lean resistance-trained athletes in a caloric deficit.
ISSN 2017: higher intakes (2.3-3.1 g/kg FFM) may be needed to maximise lean mass retention during hypocaloric periods in resistance-trained subjects.
Higher protein matters most with larger deficits and leaner individuals.

key_numbers.context: lean trained athletes in a deficit
general muscle-building intake as a floor

key_studies.citation: Helms ER, Zinn C, Rowlands DS, Brown SR. A systematic review of dietary protein during caloric restriction in resistance trained lean athletes: a case for higher intakes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2014;24(2):127-138.
Jager R et al. ISSN position stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20.
Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20.

items.source: Helms et al. 2014 (IJSNEM); ISSN position stand: protein and exercise (2017)
items.notes: Expressed per kg fat-free mass in the sources; per kg body weight equivalents depend on body fat.

items.question: How much protein can my body use for muscle building in one meal?

reference.recommendation: There is no hard 20-30 g cap. A practical target is about 0.4 g/kg per meal across at least 4 meals to reach about 1.6 g/kg/day; larger single doses are still used, and recent work shows a larger and longer anabolic response with bigger doses.
key_points: Schoenfeld & Aragon 2018: 0.4 g/kg/meal over a minimum of 4 meals, reaching 1.6 g/kg/day.
ISSN 2017: about 0.25 g/kg (20-40 g) per dose to maximise muscle protein synthesis acutely.
Trommelen 2023: 100 g of protein produced a larger and more prolonged anabolic response than 25 g.

key_studies.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Aragon AA. How much protein can the body use in a single meal for muscle-building? Implications for daily protein distribution. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2018;15:10.

Trommelen J, van Lieshout GAA, Nyakayiru J, et al. The anabolic response to protein ingestion during recovery from exercise has no upper limit in magnitude and duration in vivo in humans. Cell Rep Med. 2023;4(12):101324.
Jager R et al. ISSN position stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20.

items.source: Schoenfeld & Aragon 2018 (JISSN); ISSN 2017 protein position stand

items.question: Do I need to eat protein within 30 minutes after training (the anabolic window)?

reference.recommendation: No. Total daily protein matters far more than precise timing; when total protein is matched, timing protein around the workout shows no meaningful extra hypertrophy. Having a protein meal within a few hours before or after training is a sensible default.
key_points: Schoenfeld 2013 meta-analysis: the apparent timing effect disappeared once total protein intake was accounted for.
Aragon & Schoenfeld 2013: the post-exercise window is wide and depends on the pre-exercise meal.

key_studies.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Aragon AA, Krieger JW. The effect of protein timing on muscle strength and hypertrophy: a meta-analysis. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2013;10:53.
Aragon AA, Schoenfeld BJ. Nutrient timing revisited: is there a post-exercise anabolic window? J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2013;10:5.
Kerksick CM, Arent S, Schoenfeld BJ, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:33.

items.source: Schoenfeld, Aragon & Krieger 2013 (JISSN) meta-analysis; ISSN nutrient timing position stand 2017

items.question: Does eating casein protein before bed help build more muscle?

reference.recommendation: Pre-sleep protein (about 30-40 g of casein) raises overnight muscle protein synthesis, and one training study found larger gains, but it is unclear whether it helps beyond simply eating more total protein; it is a reasonable way to reach your daily target.
key_points: Res 2012: 40 g casein before sleep increased overnight muscle protein synthesis after evening exercise.
Snijders 2015: pre-sleep protein supplementation during 12 weeks of training increased muscle and strength gains, but total protein intake was not matched.

key_studies.citation: Res PT, Groen B, Pennings B, et al. Protein ingestion before sleep improves postexercise overnight recovery. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2012;44(8):1560-1569.

Snijders T, Res PT, Smeets JS, et al. Protein ingestion before sleep increases muscle mass and strength gains during prolonged resistance-type exercise training in healthy young men. J Nutr. 2015;145(6):1178-1184.

items.source: Res et al. 2012 (MSSE); Snijders et al. 2015 (J Nutr)

items.question: Can I build as much muscle on a vegan diet as on an omnivorous diet?

reference.recommendation: Yes, when total protein is high enough (about 1.6 g/kg/day) a vegan diet supported similar gains to an omnivorous diet in a controlled trial; plant proteins are somewhat less anabolic per gram, so aim for the upper end of protein targets and varied or blended sources.
key_points: Hevia-Larrain 2021: habitual vegans and omnivores at about 1.6 g/kg/day had similar gains over 12 weeks.
Soy vs animal protein supplementation: no difference in muscle gains (Messina 2018).
Some meta-analyses report a small lean-mass advantage for animal protein, mostly in younger adults.

key_studies.citation: Hevia-Larrain V, Gualano B, Longobardi I, et al. High-protein plant-based diet versus a protein-matched omnivorous diet to support resistance training adaptations: a comparison between habitual vegans and omnivores. Sports Med. 2021;51(6):1317-1330.

Messina M, Lynch H, Dickinson JM, Reed KE. No difference between the effects of supplementing with soy protein versus animal protein on gains in muscle mass and strength in response to resistance exercise. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(6):674-685.

items.source: Hevia-Larrain et al. 2021 (Sports Med)

items.question: How much protein should older adults eat to keep their muscle?

reference.recommendation: More than the 0.8 g/kg/day RDA: at least about 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day for healthy older adults, and around 1.2 g/kg/day or more when combined with resistance training, which is the main driver of muscle gain.
key_points: PROT-AGE (Bauer 2013): 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day for healthy older adults; at least 1.2 g/kg/day for those who exercise.
Nunes 2022: in people 65 or older doing resistance exercise, 1.2-1.59 g/kg/day increased lean mass.
RDA is 0.8 g/kg/day.

key_studies.citation: Bauer J, Biolo G, Cederholm T, et al. Evidence-based recommendations for optimal dietary protein intake in older people: a position paper from the PROT-AGE Study Group. J Am Med Dir Assoc. 2013;14(8):542-559.
Nunes EA et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults. J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle. 2022;13(2):795-810.

items.source: PROT-AGE Study Group position paper (Bauer et al. 2013); Nunes et al. 2022

items.question: Is a high-protein diet bad for my kidneys if I'm healthy?

reference.recommendation: In healthy adults, higher protein intakes have not been shown to harm kidney function; changes in kidney function markers did not differ from lower-protein diets in a meta-analysis. People with existing kidney disease are a different case and should ask their doctor.
key_points: Devries 2018 meta-analysis: changes in GFR did not differ between higher- and lower/normal-protein diets in healthy adults.
ISSN 2017: no evidence of harm from high protein intakes in healthy exercising individuals.

key_studies.citation: Devries MC, Sithamparapillai A, Brimble KS, et al. Changes in kidney function do not differ between healthy adults consuming higher- compared with lower- or normal-protein diets: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Nutr. 2018;148(11):1760-1775.
Jager R et al. ISSN position stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20.

items.source: Devries et al. 2018 (J Nutr); ISSN 2017

items.question: Do protein shakes increase muscle growth if I already eat enough protein from food?

reference.recommendation: Protein supplements help mainly by raising total protein intake; once you reach about 1.6 g/kg/day, additional supplemental protein adds little. Their average effect on fat-free mass across trials is modest.
key_points: Morton 2018: supplementation modestly increased gains in fat-free mass (about 0.3 kg) and 1RM strength (about 2.5 kg), with benefits plateauing around 1.6 g/kg/day total intake.

key_numbers.context: intake beyond which more protein added little

key_studies.citation: Morton RW et al. Protein supplementation meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(6):376-384.

items.source: Morton et al. 2018 (Br J Sports Med)
items.notes: The 0.30 kg and 2.49 kg figures are recalled from the abstract (medium confidence).

items.question: Does creatine help build muscle and strength?

reference.recommendation: Yes. Creatine monohydrate is the most effective supplement for increasing lean mass and strength alongside resistance training; take 3-5 g per day (optionally loading with about 0.3 g/kg/day, roughly 20 g/day, for 5-7 days).
key_points: ISSN 2017 position stand: creatine monohydrate is the most effective ergogenic supplement for high-intensity exercise capacity and lean mass.
Maintenance 3-5 g/day; loading about 0.3 g/kg/day for 5-7 days.

key_studies.citation: Kreider RB, Kalman DS, Antonio J, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in exercise, sport, and medicine. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:18.
Antonio J, Candow DG, Forbes SC, et al. Common questions and misconceptions about creatine supplementation: what does the scientific evidence really show? J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021;18:13.

items.source: ISSN position stand: creatine (Kreider et al. 2017)

items.question: Is long-term creatine use safe for healthy adults, or does it damage the kidneys?

reference.recommendation: Creatine monohydrate is safe for healthy adults at recommended doses, including long-term use; controlled trials show no kidney damage in healthy people. Isolated case reports and animal studies do not outweigh the trial evidence.
key_points: ISSN 2017: short- and long-term supplementation (up to 30 g/day for 5 years) is safe and well tolerated in healthy individuals.
Antonio 2021: creatine does not cause kidney damage in healthy individuals.
A false-balance trap: case reports and rat studies should not turn this into a debate.

key_studies.citation: Kreider RB et al. ISSN position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:18.
Antonio J et al. Common questions and misconceptions about creatine supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021;18:13.

items.source: ISSN position stand: creatine (Kreider et al. 2017); Antonio et al. 2021
items.notes: Calibration probe for the false-balance rule: expected consensus.

items.question: Do I need a loading phase when I start taking creatine?

reference.recommendation: No. Loading (about 20 g/day for 5-7 days) saturates muscle creatine faster, but 3-5 g/day reaches the same saturation within about 3-4 weeks.
key_points: Hultman 1996: a low daily dose (3 g/day) reached similar muscle creatine levels after about 28 days as a 6-day loading protocol.
ISSN 2017 lists both approaches.

key_studies.citation: Hultman E, Soderlund K, Timmons JA, Cederblad G, Greenhaff PL. Muscle creatine loading in men. J Appl Physiol. 1996;81(1):232-237.
Kreider RB et al. ISSN position stand: creatine. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:18.

items.source: ISSN creatine position stand 2017; Hultman et al. 1996

items.question: Does creatine cause hair loss?

reference.recommendation: There is no good evidence that creatine causes hair loss. The concern traces to a single study in rugby players that reported a rise in DHT; it did not measure hair loss and has not been replicated.
key_points: van der Merwe 2009: DHT rose with creatine loading in 20 rugby players; hair was not assessed.
Antonio 2021: current evidence does not indicate that creatine causes hair loss; confidence is limited by few studies.

key_studies.citation: van der Merwe J, Brooks NE, Myburgh KH. Three weeks of creatine monohydrate supplementation affects dihydrotestosterone to testosterone ratio in college-aged rugby players. Clin J Sport Med. 2009;19(5):399-404.
Antonio J et al. Common questions and misconceptions about creatine supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021;18:13.

items.source: Antonio et al. 2021 (JISSN)
items.notes: Expected confidence is low-to-moderate: absence of evidence, few studies.

items.question: Can I keep building muscle while I'm in a calorie deficit?

reference.recommendation: It is possible, especially for beginners, returning lifters or people with more body fat, but energy deficits blunt lean-mass gains; a meta-regression found a deficit of about 500 kcal/day prevented them, while strength gains were preserved. Keep the deficit moderate, protein high and training hard.
key_points: Murphy & Koehler 2022: lean mass gains impaired in a deficit (ES -0.57), strength gains comparable (ES -0.31, not significant).
Meta-regression: about 500 kcal/day deficit prevented lean mass gains.
Recomposition is more likely in untrained, detrained or overfat individuals.

key_numbers.context: deficit that prevented lean mass gains

key_studies.citation: Murphy C, Koehler K. Energy deficiency impairs resistance training gains in lean mass but not strength: a meta-analysis and meta-regression. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2022;32(1):125-137.
Barakat C, Pearson J, Escalante G, Campbell B, De Souza EO. Body recomposition: can trained individuals build muscle and lose fat at the same time? Strength Cond J. 2020;42(5):7-21.

items.source: Murphy & Koehler 2022 (Scand J Med Sci Sports)

items.question: How fast should I lose weight on a cut to hold on to muscle?

reference.recommendation: Aim for a slow-to-moderate rate of about 0.5-1% of body weight per week; slower loss preserved more lean mass in athletes than faster loss.
key_points: Garthe 2011: athletes losing about 0.7% of body weight per week gained lean mass, those losing 1.4% per week did not.
Helms 2014 (JISSN): 0.5-1% of body weight per week to maximise muscle retention.

key_studies.citation: Garthe I, Raastad T, Refsnes PE, Koivisto A, Sundgot-Borgen J. Effect of two different weight-loss rates on body composition and strength and power-related performance in elite athletes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2011;21(2):97-104.
Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20.

items.source: Helms, Aragon & Fitschen 2014 (JISSN); Garthe et al. 2011

items.question: How fast should I gain weight when bulking to build muscle without too much fat?

reference.recommendation: A modest surplus is enough: gaining roughly 0.25-0.5% of body weight per week is a common evidence-informed target for trained lifters, with faster gain adding mostly fat; the direct evidence is limited.
key_points: Iraki 2019 narrative review: target about 0.25-0.5% of body weight per week, and a modest surplus.
Few controlled trials compare surplus sizes in trained lifters.

key_studies.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition recommendations for bodybuilders in the off-season: a narrative review. Sports. 2019;7(7):154.

items.source: Iraki et al. 2019 (Sports, narrative review)
items.notes: Low-certainty evidence; the reference is a narrative review.

items.question: Is a low-carb diet better than a low-fat diet for losing fat?

reference.recommendation: Neither is meaningfully better for fat loss when calories and protein are matched; choose the one you can sustain.
key_points: DIETFITS (Gardner 2018): 609 adults, 12 months, no significant difference in weight loss between healthy low-fat and healthy low-carb diets.
ISSN position stand on diets and body composition (Aragon 2017): with protein and calories equated, diets give similar fat loss.

key_studies.citation: Gardner CD, Trepanowski JF, Del Gobbo LC, et al. Effect of low-fat vs low-carbohydrate diet on 12-month weight loss in overweight adults and the association with genotype pattern or insulin secretion: the DIETFITS randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2018;319(7):667-679.
Aragon AA, Schoenfeld BJ, Wildman R, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets and body composition. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:16.

items.source: DIETFITS (Gardner et al. 2018, JAMA); ISSN position stand: diets and body composition (2017)

items.question: Does eating more frequent small meals help me lose more fat?

reference.recommendation: No. With calories equated, meal frequency has no meaningful effect on fat loss or body composition; pick a meal pattern that helps you control intake and spread protein.
key_points: Schoenfeld 2015 meta-analysis: an apparent small benefit of higher frequency disappeared in sensitivity analysis (driven by one study).

key_studies.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Aragon AA, Krieger JW. Effects of meal frequency on weight loss and body composition: a meta-analysis. Nutr Rev. 2015;73(2):69-82.

items.source: Schoenfeld, Aragon & Krieger 2015 (Nutr Rev)

items.question: Is fasted cardio better for fat loss than cardio after eating?

reference.recommendation: No. With matched calorie deficits, fasted and fed cardio produce similar fat loss; do whichever you prefer.
key_points: Schoenfeld 2014 RCT: similar fat loss fasted vs fed in a hypocaloric diet.
Meta-analysis (Hackett & Hagstrom 2017): no difference in weight or fat loss.

key_studies.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Aragon AA, Wilborn CD, Krieger JW, Sonmez GT. Body composition changes associated with fasted versus non-fasted aerobic exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:54.
Hackett D, Hagstrom AD. Effect of overnight fasted exercise on weight loss and body composition: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. 2017;2(4):43.

items.source: Schoenfeld et al. 2014 (JISSN); Hackett & Hagstrom 2017

items.question: Will 16:8 intermittent fasting make me lose muscle if I keep lifting?

reference.recommendation: Probably not, if you keep training and eat enough protein: time-restricted eating with resistance training generally maintained lean mass and strength while reducing fat, though some trials saw smaller lean-mass gains than normal eating patterns.
key_points: Moro 2016: 8 weeks of 16/8 time-restricted feeding in resistance-trained men reduced fat mass and maintained fat-free mass and strength.
Some trials report blunted lean-mass gains with TRE when protein or energy is lower.

key_studies.citation: Moro T, Tinsley G, Bianco A, et al. Effects of eight weeks of time-restricted feeding (16/8) on basal metabolism, maximal strength, body composition, inflammation, and cardiovascular risk factors in resistance-trained males. J Transl Med. 2016;14:290.

items.source: Moro et al. 2016 (J Transl Med)
items.notes: Limited evidence; leaning is the expected status.

items.question: I can only train 3 days a week. Should I do full-body sessions or a split?

reference.recommendation: Either can work if weekly volume per muscle is the same; with only 3 days, full-body sessions make it easy to train each muscle about 2-3 times per week and spread the sets, which is a practical default.
key_points: With volume equated, frequency does not change hypertrophy much (Schoenfeld 2019).
Training each muscle at least twice weekly helps when volume is not equated (Schoenfeld 2016).

key_studies.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J, Krieger J. How many times per week should a muscle be trained to maximize muscle hypertrophy? J Sports Sci. 2019;37(11):1286-1295.
Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW. Effects of resistance training frequency on measures of muscle hypertrophy. Sports Med. 2016;46(11):1689-1697.

items.source: Schoenfeld et al. 2019 and 2016 frequency meta-analyses

items.question: How many sets per week do I need to maximize strength gains?

reference.recommendation: Multiple sets beat single sets, but strength gains level off at lower volumes than hypertrophy; roughly 5-10 hard weekly sets per lift or muscle captures most of the strength benefit, with heavy loads mattering more than extra volume.
key_points: Ralston 2017: moderate and higher weekly set volumes produced larger strength gains than low volumes.
Schoenfeld 2019: higher volume increased hypertrophy but not strength in trained men.
Dose-response meta-regressions show strength gains plateau quickly with volume.

key_numbers.context: range capturing most of the strength benefit (approximate)

key_studies.citation: Ralston GW, Kilgore L, Wyatt FB, Baker JS. The effect of weekly set volume on strength gain: a meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2017;47(12):2585-2601.
Schoenfeld BJ et al. Resistance training volume enhances muscle hypertrophy but not strength in trained men. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019;51(1):94-103.

items.source: Ralston et al. 2017 (Sports Med); Schoenfeld et al. 2019 (MSSE)
items.notes: The 5-10 range is an approximate synthesis, not a figure from one paper; the judge should focus on the direction (diminishing returns, load matters more).
